soil-class-155.title: Aquic conditions: soil that runs out of oxygen
soil-class-155.text: A few days of saturation each year is enough to change a soil's label. Aquic conditions describe a {{ref:soil-class-011}} in which the soil stays saturated long enough to become virtually free of dissolved oxygen. In plain terms, every pore fills with water, the measure tracked by {{ref:soil-water-166}}. The telltale marks are {{ref:soil-chem-120}}. Clay-rich {{ref:soil-class-106}} soils often show them for some time in most years, because heavy clay slows the passage of water. Many {{ref:soil-class-098}} soils show aquic conditions too, unless they have been artificially drained.

soil-class-154.title: The aridic regime, where soil stays dry
soil-class-154.text: In arid and semi-arid climates, soil is dry for at least half the growing season. That defines the aridic moisture regime, also called torric. The soil is moist for less than 90 consecutive days. Its control section sits at 50 cm depth, and dry and moist days count only when the soil is warmer than 5 °C and 8 °C. The ustic regime is wetter than the aridic and drier than the udic. The desert soil order, {{ref:soil-class-093}}, must have an aridic regime. The torric name reappears in groups such as Torripsamments, members of {{ref:soil-class-108}} with an aridic regime.

soil-class-152.title: ISO 14688, the engineer's international soil yardstick
soil-class-152.text: An engineer in one country needs to call a soil by the same name as an engineer in another. ISO 14688 is the international standard that sets basic principles for identifying and classifying soils for {{ref:soil-class-002}}. Part 1 covers natural soils in place, similar man-made materials and soils redeposited by people. It grades clay as particles smaller than 2 μm. Sand splits into fine, medium and coarse at 0.063, 0.2, 0.63 and 2.0 mm. Gravel follows at 2, 6.3, 20 and 63 mm. The system closely resembles the Unified Soil Classification System, but it codes soils differently and adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

soil-class-153.title: The xeric regime of Mediterranean soils
soil-class-153.text: Cool, moist winters and warm, dry summers mark the Mediterranean climate, and its soils carry the xeric moisture regime. Like the ustic regime, it brings long summer droughts. The regime lends its name to whole groups of soils in USDA taxonomy. Xerolls are Mediterranean examples of {{ref:soil-class-101}}, and Xeralfs belong to {{ref:soil-class-090}}. Greek examples of {{ref:soil-class-058}} fall partly in Rhodoxeralfs, Palexeralfs and Xerochrepts, xeric members of those orders and of {{ref:soil-class-100}}.

soil-class-162.title: Five ways to be an Ultisol
soil-class-162.text: Not all {{ref:soil-class-104}} soils behave alike. {{ref:soil-class-006}} splits them into five suborders by wetness, organic matter and climate. Aquults have a water table at or near the surface for much of the year. Udults belong to humid climates and Ustults to semiarid and subhumid ones. Xerults are temperate, with arid summers and moist winters. Humults stand apart: well drained and rich in organic matter, they are relatively fertile, as in the Olympic series. Each suborder seeds longer names below it. The Cecil series is a Typic Kanhapludult, the Bama series a Typic Paleudult.

soil-class-161.title: Calcids, desert soils cemented with carbonate
soil-class-161.text: Too little rain falls on a Calcid to wash its lime away. This suborder of {{ref:soil-class-093}} has piled up high levels of calcium carbonate, either left from carbonate-rich parent material or delivered as dust. Rainfall has been too low to remove it or carry it deep. The result is a {{ref:soil-form-121}}, a hypercalcic horizon or a {{ref:soil-form-029}} whose top lies within 1.0 m of the surface. Most Calcids serve as rangeland or wildlife habitat. Where they are irrigated for crops, micronutrient deficiency is normal. Great groups include Salicalcids, Gypsicalcids, Petrocalcids, Hypercalcids and Haplocalcids.

soil-class-157.title: Constructed soil, built to bring dead ground back
soil-class-157.text: A spent mine or a capped landfill has no usable topsoil left. Constructed soil fills that gap: a designed mixture of organic and mineral materials, often including repurposed organic waste, made to approximate natural soil and grow plants. Such soils are classed as {{ref:soil-class-145}}. They beat imported {{ref:soil-form-021}}, because harvesting topsoil degrades a second site and usually costs more. A mineral fraction sets texture, an organic fraction supplies nutrients, and a slowly decomposing carbon source, such as wood chips or {{ref:soil-fert-050}}, lasts longer. Organic matter in the top layer should not exceed 15% by weight, or the soil settles and waterlogs. A {{ref:soil-fert-184}} near 20:1 releases nutrients steadily. Layers thicker than about 45 cm can mimic natural {{ref:soil-found-001}} layers, with a sand or gravel drainage layer. Abrupt changes between layers decide whether water flows sideways or down, and where it perches. Living organisms and stable structure come later, as plants return. Every batch must meet legal limits for pathogens, harmful trace elements, salinity and pH.

soil-class-156.title: The acrotelm, a bog's living upper skin
soil-class-156.text: An undisturbed {{ref:soil-class-070}} bog, a {{ref:soil-water-121}}, has two layers, and only the upper one is alive. The acrotelm holds the living plants and overlies the deeper catotelm. The water table rises and falls within it, so conditions swing between airy and airless. Its lower edge usually matches the water table's lowest level. Water moves through it more easily than through the layer below, and it is less dense. Ditching before peat harvest thickens and dries it. A fully developed acrotelm, found only in bogs fed by rain alone, lets researchers study what falls from the atmosphere.

soil-class-158.title: Machair, grassland built from broken seashells
soil-class-158.text: On the Outer Hebrides, waves roll shell fragments ashore, break them up and the wind blows them inland. William MacGillivray first proposed this origin in 1830 for machair, a fertile, low-lying dune grassland on north-western coasts of Ireland and Scotland. The beaches hold 20% to 80% calcium carbonate, making machair a strongly {{ref:soil-chem-035}}, with pH typically above 7. Yet the sand holds nutrients poorly and lacks copper, cobalt and manganese. Cattle need supplements, and only some oats, rye and bere barley thrive. Early farmers spread seaweed, and buried kelp composted into fertile beds.

soil-class-159.title: Black cotton soil of the Deccan Plateau
soil-class-159.text: Lava flows of the Deccan traps gave India about 300,000 square kilometres of black, clayey soil. Called black cotton soil, or regur, it covers the north-western Deccan Plateau and takes its name from its suitability for cotton. It is rich in {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, so it retains water well, and it holds calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime. In hot, dry spells it cracks, which lets air in. Dry, it is very hard; wet, it turns to mud, so it needs deep {{ref:soil-agri-095}} to drain. Engineers find it highly compressible, with low bearing capacity and low shear strength.

soil-class-160.title: Paddy soil, where flooded rice breeds methane
soil-class-160.text: Flooding a rice field changes the soil beneath it. Paddy soil, the soil of flooded {{ref:soil-chem-133}} plots, counts among the soils shaped by people, alongside the {{ref:soil-class-120}} group. Organic matter decomposes there without oxygen, and methane-making microbes thrive, through {{ref:soil-chem-129}}. They keep working even though the soil is temporarily oxygenated. One analysis of its fatty-acid markers found the bacteria and archaea about 44% aerobic bacteria, 32% facultative anaerobes and 24% archaea. Paddy soils can also be superbly productive. The smectite-rich ones of Thailand's Central Plains rank among the most productive in the world.
